tasks.prompt: Order the establishment of a utility wide drinking water quality management system.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Class 4 utility in Alberta building a formal quality management system for all treatment operations under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: leadership commitment through the management system in routine use.

cards.label: Secure a written commitment and policy from utility leadership that names quality responsibilities and resources
Map every process from source intake to treated water delivery and assign an owner to each process
Write the procedures, records, and competence requirements for each owned process
Train all affected staff on their procedures and verify understanding with supervised practice
Run the system for one full operating quarter and collect records, deviations, and staff feedback
Hold a leadership review of the quarter results and approve the system for ongoing use with assigned improvements

tasks.explanation: A management system starts with leadership commitment and clear process ownership, and it is only real once records from a full quarter have been reviewed and improved.

tasks.prompt: Order the annual management review cycle for a drinking water utility.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility leadership team in Saskatchewan running its yearly review of treatment performance under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: review inputs gathered through actions tracked to completion.

cards.label: Collect the year inputs: quality results, audit findings, incidents, customer concerns, and process performance trends
Analyse the inputs for recurring causes and for risks that are growing rather than single events
Present the analysis to utility leadership with options and resource needs for each major issue
Record leadership decisions, owners, and due dates for every accepted improvement action
Fund and schedule the accepted actions in the operating and capital plans for the coming year
Track the actions quarterly and report completion and effect at the next annual review

tasks.explanation: Management review turns a year of records into funded, owned decisions, and tracking to the next review is what separates a review from a meeting.

tasks.prompt: Order an internal audit program for treatment operations.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Class 4 utility in Manitoba auditing its own treatment procedures before any external review under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: audit plan through verified corrective actions.

cards.label: Set the audit scope and schedule so every critical treatment process is audited within the cycle
Select and train auditors who do not audit their own work and give them the procedure and record checklists
Conduct the audits by observing work, interviewing operators, and sampling records for each process
Classify each finding by treated water quality risk and agree the facts with the process owner
Require a corrective action plan with an owner and a due date for every significant finding
Verify each corrective action in the field and close the finding only when the fix is working

tasks.explanation: Internal audits protect quality only when findings are risk ranked, owned, and verified in the field, not when they are simply filed.

tasks.prompt: Order a corrective action and preventive action program for a utility.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional regional utility in British Columbia handling deviations from lab results, alarms, and audits under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: deviation reported through systemic causes removed.

cards.label: Define which deviations, near misses, and audit findings must enter the corrective action system
Log each entry with the immediate containment taken to protect treated water quality
Investigate significant entries for root cause using records, trends, and operator interviews
Approve corrective and preventive actions that address the root cause, with owners and due dates
Implement the actions and update any procedures, training, or equipment the cause points to
Check effectiveness after a set operating period and reopen the entry if the deviation recurs

tasks.explanation: Containment protects water today, root cause work prevents the repeat, and the effectiveness check proves the difference.

tasks.prompt: Order a document and records control system for treatment operations.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Class 4 utility in Alberta where several procedure versions are in use at once under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: document inventory through controlled documents in daily use.

cards.label: Inventory all procedures, forms, and drawings and identify which version is actually in use at each location
Assign each controlled document an owner, a version number, and a scheduled review date
Approve current versions through the designated authority and withdraw every superseded copy
Place the approved versions where operators work and train staff on any changed procedure
Set retention rules for operating and quality records so they stay retrievable for reviews and inspections
Audit document use after one quarter and correct any location still using an uncontrolled copy

tasks.explanation: Document control fails at the point of use, so withdrawal of old copies and a field audit matter as much as approving the new version.

tasks.prompt: Order the development and approval of a utility drinking water quality policy.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility board in Saskatchewan adopting its first formal quality policy under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: drafting principles through the policy communicated and applied.

cards.label: Gather input from operators, laboratory staff, and leadership on the commitments the policy must carry
Draft the policy around safe water, regulatory compliance in general terms, competence, and continual improvement
Check the draft against current procedures to find commitments the utility cannot yet meet
Close the gaps with funded actions or revise the draft so every commitment is achievable
Approve the policy at the highest utility level and sign and date the approved version
Communicate the policy to all staff and the public summary, and test it in the next management review

tasks.explanation: A quality policy is credible only when it is checked against real capability before approval, so the commitments signed are ones the utility can keep.

tasks.prompt: Order a senior operator accountability and delegation framework for a multi plant utility.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Manitoba operating three treatment plants with shared senior staff under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: accountability gaps identified through delegations tested in practice.

cards.label: List the decisions and duties that must always have a named accountable senior operator, including after hours
Map current coverage by plant and by hour and mark every gap or single person dependency
Write delegation rules that state who acts when the accountable operator is absent and what limits apply
Confirm each named operator holds the certification and experience the delegation requires
Brief all shifts and post the delegation roster where control room staff can reach it at any hour
Test the framework with an after hours scenario exercise and correct the gaps it reveals

tasks.explanation: Accountability that exists only on weekday day shift is not accountability, so the framework is tested after hours before it is trusted.

tasks.prompt: Order a management of change program for treatment process changes.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Class 4 plant in British Columbia where chemical, equipment, and set point changes have been informal under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: change triggers defined through changes reviewed after implementation.

cards.label: Define which changes need formal review, including chemicals, equipment, software, procedures, and staffing of critical roles
Require a change request that states the reason, the quality and safety risks, and the rollback plan
Review each request with operations, maintenance, laboratory, and safety staff before approval
Approve, schedule, and communicate the change with any training or procedure updates completed first
Implement the change under supervision and monitor the affected quality results closely at first
Review the change after a set period and close it, extend monitoring, or roll it back on the evidence

tasks.explanation: Management of change puts the risk review and the training before the change, and the post change review decides whether the change has earned its place.

tasks.prompt: Order the preparation of an annual drinking water report for the utility governing body.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Alberta reporting a full year of treatment performance to its council or board under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: data assembled through the report received and actions directed.

cards.label: Assemble the year quality results, production volumes, incidents, and compliance related summaries in general terms
Reconcile the report figures with laboratory records and plant logs so every number can be traced to its source
Draft the report in plain language with trends, explanations for adverse results, and corrective actions taken
Have senior operations and laboratory staff review the draft for accuracy before leadership sign off
Present the report to the governing body and record its questions, directions, and any requested follow up
Publish the public version and file the presentation record with the year quality file

tasks.explanation: An annual report earns trust when its figures trace to source records and adverse results are explained with the actions taken, not omitted.

tasks.prompt: Order a utility strategic plan refresh for drinking water services.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional regional utility in Saskatchewan setting a five year direction for treatment services under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: current state assessment through the refreshed plan adopted and resourced.

cards.label: Assess the current state: asset condition, quality performance, capacity, workforce, and financial position
Scan the drivers that will shape the next five years, including growth, climate, source risk, and technology change
Set a small number of strategic goals with a measurable outcome for each one
Build initiatives under each goal with owners, sequencing, and the resources each initiative needs
Test the draft plan against the capital and operating forecasts and remove or defer what cannot be funded
Adopt the plan at leadership level and review progress against it twice a year

tasks.explanation: A strategic plan that is not tested against funding is a wish list, so affordability is checked before adoption and progress is reviewed on a fixed cycle.

tasks.prompt: Order a senior decision routine for major operating decisions under uncertainty.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility leadership team in Saskatchewan formalizing how it decides when evidence is incomplete under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: decision triggers defined through decisions reviewed for quality, not only outcome.

cards.label: Define the decision classes that must come to the senior routine: quality risk, major spending in general terms, service interruption, and public communication
Require each proposal to state the evidence, the uncertainty, the options, and the cost of waiting
Set the rule that the operator closest to the problem presents first and seniority speaks after the facts
Decide with a recorded rationale, the dissent noted, and the conditions that would reopen the decision
Assign the implementation owner and the date the decision effect will be checked
Review past decisions for the quality of their reasoning at the time, and improve the routine from what the reviews teach

tasks.explanation: Decisions under uncertainty are judged by the quality of their reasoning with the evidence then available, and recording dissent and reopening conditions keeps the routine honest.

tasks.prompt: Order the development of a utility wide water quality strategy.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Class 4 utility in Manitoba setting a multi year quality strategy from source to treated water under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: quality risks profiled through the strategy adopted with funded priorities.

cards.label: Profile quality risks at each barrier: source, treatment, storage, and treated water leaving the plant
Set measurable quality goals for each barrier that go beyond minimum compliance in general terms
Identify the gaps between current performance and each goal using trend data and audit results
Rank the gaps by health risk and by how many people are affected when performance slips
Build a funded improvement program for the highest ranked gaps with owners and milestones
Adopt the strategy at leadership level and report progress against the goals every quarter

tasks.explanation: A quality strategy ranks gaps by health risk rather than by ease, and quarterly reporting keeps the funded program tied to the goals it was built for.

tasks.prompt: Order a source to tap multi barrier risk review for a utility.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in British Columbia reviewing every barrier on a river source system under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: hazards inventoried through barrier gaps closed or formally accepted.

cards.label: Inventory hazards and hazardous events at the source, intake, each treatment step, and storage
For each hazard, record the barrier that controls it and the evidence that the barrier works
Score the residual risk where barriers are weak, unmonitored, or dependent on one person or one device
Rank the residual risks and assign each significant one an owner and a treatment option
Implement the chosen controls or formally accept the risk at leadership level with a review date
Re score the risks after controls are in place and file the review as the utility risk register for water quality

tasks.explanation: A barrier review trusts evidence, not habit: a barrier without monitoring or backup carries residual risk no matter how long it has worked.

tasks.prompt: Order a long term disinfection strategy for a utility with several plants.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional multi plant utility in Alberta balancing inactivation, residuals, and byproducts across different sources under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: plant by plant barrier assessment through one utility strategy in service.

cards.label: Assess each plant barriers, credits in general terms, contact conditions, and byproduct history
Identify the weakest plant and condition combinations, such as cold water, high organics, and peak flow together
Compare strategy options for each weak point, including ultraviolet, chlorine sequencing, and organics removal
Select a utility standard approach with plant specific set points where sources genuinely differ
Stage the changes so no plant loses a barrier during conversion and verify credit conditions at each stage
Adopt the strategy, brief all plants, and trend inactivation margins and byproducts together quarterly

tasks.explanation: Disinfection strategy is set at the weakest combined condition across the fleet, and inactivation and byproducts are trended together so one is never bought with the other.

tasks.prompt: Order a disinfection byproduct control strategy for the next five years.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Saskatchewan with rising byproduct trends on a high organics prairie source under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: byproduct drivers confirmed through the long term control program adopted.

cards.label: Trend byproduct results with raw organics, chlorine dose, water age, and temperature to confirm the true drivers
Set a byproduct control goal with margin below the guideline values referenced in general terms
Evaluate control options in order: source and organics removal first, then dose and point of application, then distribution age
Pilot the leading option at the worst plant or season and measure byproducts at the strategy sampling points
Adopt the proven program as seasonal operating rules with dose and organics targets by raw condition
Review results each season and adjust the program before trends approach the internal goal

tasks.explanation: Byproducts are controlled at their drivers, starting with organics, and the program acts on trends with margin rather than waiting for a limit to be reached.

tasks.prompt: Order a corrosion control strategy review for treated water quality.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Manitoba reviewing treated water stability and metals results at consumer taps in general terms under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: stability data reviewed through the revised treatment targets in service.

cards.label: Collect treated water pH, alkalinity, hardness, and tap metals results for a full seasonal cycle
Assess water stability using the utility indices and compare results across seasons and plants
Identify whether instability comes from source chemistry, treatment targets, or blending between plants
Select revised pH and alkalinity targets and the chemical changes needed to hold them
Trial the revised targets at one plant and monitor tap results and treatment side effects for a season
Adopt the proven targets utility wide and set the ongoing tap monitoring and review schedule

tasks.explanation: Corrosion control is proven at the tap over a season, not at the plant on one day, so targets are trialled and monitored where the water is actually used.

tasks.prompt: Order an emerging contaminant readiness strategy.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Class 4 utility in British Columbia preparing for contaminants of emerging concern in its source under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: source vulnerability assessed through a readiness plan with trigger levels.

cards.label: Screen the source watershed for activities and discharges that could introduce contaminants of emerging concern
Review current guideline and provincial information in general terms for the contaminants most relevant to the source
Check which relevant contaminants the current treatment barriers can and cannot reduce, using supplier and literature evidence
Set a monitoring approach with sampling points, frequencies, and accredited laboratory arrangements
Define trigger levels and the leadership decisions each trigger starts, including treatment changes and public communication
Adopt the readiness plan, brief senior staff, and review it whenever source activities or guidance change

tasks.explanation: Readiness means the monitoring, the treatment evidence, and the decisions are agreed before a detection, so the first result starts a plan instead of an argument.

tasks.prompt: Order a cyanobacteria and algal toxin management strategy for a reservoir source utility.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Alberta drawing from a prairie reservoir with seasonal blooms under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: bloom risk profiled through the seasonal strategy in operation.

cards.label: Profile bloom history with reservoir temperature, nutrients, wind, and past toxin results by season
Set a surveillance program of visual checks, cell counts or indicators, and toxin sampling triggers
Confirm which treatment steps remove cells and which address dissolved toxin, and set intake depth options
Write the response levels that change intake, treatment, and sampling as bloom indicators rise
Stage the chemicals, laboratory capacity, and communications needed at the highest response level
Run the strategy through one bloom season and revise the triggers and response levels from the season record

tasks.explanation: Bloom management separates cell removal from dissolved toxin control, because a step that solves one can worsen the other if the sequence is wrong.

tasks.prompt: Order a utility taste and odour management strategy.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Saskatchewan where seasonal taste and odour complaints recur each summer under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: causes characterized through a seasonal control program adopted.

cards.label: Characterize past events by source condition, treatment state, and complaint pattern to separate source from treatment causes
Set source surveillance for algae and organics indicators ahead of the historical event window
Evaluate control options such as oxidant timing, activated carbon, and intake management for the confirmed cause
Trial the leading control at the first event of the season and judge it on treated results and complaints together
Adopt the seasonal program with start triggers, dose rules, and complaint tracking in one place
Review each season and retire controls that the evidence shows do not change the outcome

tasks.explanation: Taste and odour controls are judged on treated water and complaints together, and controls that do not change either are retired rather than repeated by habit.

tasks.prompt: Order the design of a utility compliance sampling program for a new operating year.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Class 4 utility in Manitoba designing its treated water sampling program for the year under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: requirements gathered in general terms through the approved program in the laboratory system.

cards.label: List the parameters, locations, and frequencies the provincial requirements and the utility quality goals call for in general terms
Map sampling points so source, process, treated, and storage points each answer a defined question
Assign accredited laboratory methods, holding times, and courier schedules that fit western Canadian distances
Build the calendar with backup dates and named backup samplers for illness, weather, and road closures
Have the laboratory and senior operations review the program together and approve it before the year starts
Load the approved program into the tracking system and review completion and result quality monthly

tasks.explanation: A sampling program for a western utility must survive distance and winter, so backup samplers and courier timing are designed in, not improvised.

tasks.prompt: Order a treated water storage quality strategy for a utility.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in British Columbia with several treated water reservoirs of different ages and turnover under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: storage inventory assessed through turnover and inspection rules in service.

cards.label: Inventory every storage facility with volume, age, turnover, mixing, and inspection history
Trend residual and quality results by facility to find where water age is degrading quality
Set turnover and level operating rules for each facility that protect residual without wasting treated water
Schedule cleaning and inspection by quality risk and age, with treated water isolation and disinfection steps defined
Return each cleaned facility to service only on satisfactory quality results
Adopt the strategy and review facility trends and inspection due dates at each management review

tasks.explanation: Storage quality is managed facility by facility, because turnover and age differ, and a cleaned tank returns to service on results, not on schedule.

tasks.prompt: Order a treatment technology needs assessment for a growing utility.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional growing utility in Alberta defining what a future treatment upgrade must achieve under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: future demands defined through a needs statement approved for study.

cards.label: Forecast future flows, source quality ranges, and quality goals over the planning horizon
Document where the current plant cannot meet those demands, with data for each shortfall
State the needs as performance outcomes, not as a preferred technology, so options stay open
Set the evaluation criteria and their relative weight, including quality, risk, lifecycle cost in general terms, and operability
Have operations, laboratory, and maintenance staff test the needs statement against real operating experience
Approve the needs statement at leadership level as the fixed basis for the selection study

tasks.explanation: A needs assessment states outcomes before technologies, so the later selection is judged against the problem rather than against a favourite solution.

tasks.prompt: Order a technology screening study from a long list to a short list.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Saskatchewan screening treatment options for organics and turbidity control under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: long list assembled through a defensible short list approved for piloting.

cards.label: Assemble a long list of credible technologies that could meet the approved needs statement
Apply pass or fail screens first: source fit, cold climate suitability, residuals handling, and regulatory acceptability in general terms
Score the survivors against the weighted criteria using evidence from reference plants in similar climates
Visit or interview at least one operating reference utility for each leading option
Record the scores, the evidence, and the reasons every option was kept or dropped
Approve a short list of no more than three options for pilot or detailed evaluation

tasks.explanation: Screening applies fatal flaw screens before scoring, because a weighted score must never rescue an option that cannot work in a cold western source.

tasks.prompt: Order a pilot study design for a short listed treatment technology.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Manitoba piloting a membrane system on a variable river source under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: pilot objectives set through a design that can answer the selection question.

cards.label: State the selection questions the pilot must answer, with a measurable success value for each one
Size the pilot and set its location so it sees the same source water as the full plant
Schedule the pilot across the worst source conditions, including spring runoff and cold water, not only easy months
Define the sampling, data logging, and quality checks that will prove performance and fouling behaviour
Set the operating staffing, chemical supply, and waste handling the pilot needs for the full run
Approve the pilot design and success values before equipment is ordered, and file them unchangeable without leadership sign off

tasks.explanation: A pilot proves a technology only if it runs through the worst source conditions and its success values were fixed before the results arrived.

tasks.prompt: Order the evaluation of pilot results and the scale up decision.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in British Columbia deciding whether pilot membrane results justify a full plant under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: pilot data validated through a scale up decision recorded with its conditions.

cards.label: Validate the pilot data set and exclude only periods with a documented equipment or sampling fault
Compare results with the success values fixed in the pilot design, criterion by criterion
Scale the pilot performance to full plant flows and seasons, stating every assumption the scaling uses
Update the lifecycle comparison with pilot based chemical, energy, and cleaning figures
Present the comparison and the remaining risks to leadership with a clear recommend or reject position
Record the decision and its conditions, including any further piloting a conditional approval requires

tasks.explanation: Scale up is decided against the success values set before the pilot, with scaling assumptions stated, so enthusiasm cannot quietly move the goalposts.

tasks.prompt: Order a membrane system selection study for a utility upgrade.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Alberta choosing between membrane options for a plant expansion under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: duty defined through the selected system carried into design.

cards.label: Define the duty: design flows, recovery or flux expectations in general terms, feed quality range, and treated quality goals
Require each proponent to state performance at the coldest design temperature, not only at reference temperature
Compare cleaning regimes, chemical needs, membrane life evidence, and residuals volumes for each option
Check reference plants on similar cold, high organics sources and record their fouling and replacement history
Score the options against the weighted criteria and test the ranking by varying the weights
Select the system, record the reasons, and carry its guaranteed values into the design requirements

tasks.explanation: Membrane selection in western Canada is decided at the coldest water and on cleaning and replacement evidence, because that is where lifetime cost and capacity are set.

tasks.prompt: Order an ultraviolet disinfection system selection study.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Saskatchewan adding ultraviolet disinfection as an additional barrier under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: credit goal defined in general terms through the selected system carried into design.

cards.label: Define the inactivation goal in general terms and the flow, transmittance, and water quality range it must be met across
Require validated dose delivery evidence across that range, including lamp aging and sleeve fouling allowances
Compare reactor configurations for redundancy, so the goal is met with the largest unit out of service
Assess cleaning systems, lamp replacement logistics, and power needs for a remote western site
Score the options and check the leading option against the disinfection strategy it must serve
Select the system and carry its validated operating envelope into the plant control and alarm design

tasks.explanation: Ultraviolet selection rests on validated dose across the real transmittance range with a unit out of service, not on nameplate dose at ideal water.

tasks.prompt: Order a residuals treatment technology selection for a plant with growing sludge volumes.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Manitoba choosing how to thicken and dewater treatment residuals under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: residuals characterized through the selected process carried into capital planning.

cards.label: Characterize residuals volume and solids across seasons, including the spring runoff peak
Define the required outcomes: solids capture, cake dryness in general terms, filtrate quality, and hauling limits
Screen credible thickening and dewatering options against cold climate operation and operator skill needs
Pilot or trial the leading option on real residuals, including the hardest spring material
Compare full costs in general terms, including hauling and disposal route capacity for the cake produced
Select the process and place it in the capital plan with its building and storage needs included

tasks.explanation: Residuals selection is tested on spring runoff material and includes the disposal route, because a process that works in summer can fail the utility in April.

tasks.prompt: Order a chemical system replacement selection, from bulk storage to feed.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Class 4 plant in British Columbia replacing an aging chlorine and coagulant system under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: hazards and duties defined through the selected system carried into design.

cards.label: List the chemicals, duties, storage days required, and the hazards of the current system that must be designed out
Compare credible storage and feed options for reliability, containment, delivery access in winter, and operator exposure
Check each option against current safety guidance in general terms and the plant emergency arrangements
Trial feed accuracy of the leading option across the full dose range on the bench or a temporary skid
Score the options with safety and reliability weighted ahead of first cost
Select the system and carry its containment, ventilation, and alarm requirements into the project design

tasks.explanation: Chemical systems are selected safety first, with feed accuracy proven across the dose range, because the cheapest system is the most expensive one after an incident.

tasks.prompt: Order a supervisory control system replacement selection for a utility.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional multi plant utility in Alberta replacing an unsupported control and data system under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: operational needs defined through the selected platform carried into implementation planning.

cards.label: Document what operators must see, control, trend, and report, plant by plant, before looking at products
Set non negotiable requirements: alarm handling, data retention, remote access security, and support life
Require each proponent to demonstrate the system on the utility own operating scenarios, including an alarm flood and a communications loss
Check reference utilities of similar size in western Canada for support quality and upgrade history
Score the demonstrations and references, and test how the ranking changes if support criteria are weighted higher
Select the platform and plan implementation plant by plant so no plant is left without control or records

tasks.explanation: Control systems are chosen on demonstrated behaviour during failures and on support life, because that is when the system earns or loses operator trust.

tasks.prompt: Order an innovation trial governance process for new treatment ideas.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Saskatchewan that wants staff ideas tested without risking treated water quality under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: idea intake through trials judged and scaled or stopped on evidence.

cards.label: Open a simple intake where any operator can propose a trial with the problem it addresses and the expected benefit
Screen each proposal for treated water quality and safety risk, and reject or redesign any that can reach the clearwell unguarded
Approve small trials with a defined duration, success measures, and a named trial owner
Run the trial isolated or closely monitored, with quality sampling increased for its duration
Judge the results against the success measures and record scale up, extend, or stop decisions
Share the outcome with all staff, including stopped trials, and file the lessons in the improvement program

tasks.explanation: Innovation governance protects the clearwell first and publishes stopped trials as proudly as successes, so staff keep bringing ideas forward.

tasks.prompt: Order an asset inventory and condition assessment program for treatment assets.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Class 4 utility in Manitoba building its first complete treatment asset register under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: asset hierarchy defined through condition data feeding the capital plan.

cards.label: Define the asset hierarchy from plant down to maintainable components and the data each record must carry
Field verify the inventory asset by asset, photographing nameplates and correcting the register on site
Assess condition using a standard grading scale with photo evidence for the worst grades
Record remaining life estimates and the basis for each one, separating age from observed condition
Load the verified register into the maintenance system and link work history to each asset
Use the condition results to set the inspection cycle and to feed the risk ranking for capital planning

tasks.explanation: An asset register is only useful when it is field verified and graded on observed condition, because age alone misranks both failing and healthy assets.

tasks.prompt: Order a levels of service framework for drinking water treatment.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in British Columbia defining what service its community should expect under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: community expectations gathered through service levels adopted and reported.

cards.label: Gather expectations from the governing body and the community on quality, reliability, pressure of supply in general terms, and cost awareness
Translate each expectation into a measurable service level with a target and a reporting frequency
Measure current performance against each draft service level and identify the gaps honestly
Cost the options in general terms for closing each gap and present the trade offs to the governing body
Adopt the service levels the governing body accepts and funds
Report performance against the adopted levels every year and review the levels themselves on a set cycle

tasks.explanation: Levels of service make the cost of reliability explicit, so the governing body chooses and funds a standard instead of discovering it after a failure.

tasks.prompt: Order the development of a twenty year capital plan for treatment.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Alberta planning treatment investment over twenty years under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: needs gathered through the plan adopted and updated annually.

cards.label: Collect needs from condition assessments, capacity forecasts, quality strategy gaps, and regulatory change in general terms
Group the needs into projects with a scope, a timing driver, and a consequence of deferral for each one
Sequence the projects so enabling work comes first and no project strands a later one
Build the funding profile in general terms across the twenty years and smooth the peaks where the work allows
Present the plan with the deferral consequences stated plainly for any project pushed beyond its timing driver
Adopt the plan and update it every year with completed work, new condition data, and revised forecasts

tasks.explanation: A twenty year plan sequences by timing driver and states deferral consequences plainly, so a delay is a recorded decision and not a surprise failure.

tasks.prompt: Order an asset criticality and risk ranking for capital prioritization.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Saskatchewan ranking treatment assets to decide renewal order under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: failure consequences defined through the ranked list governing renewal sequencing.

cards.label: Define consequence categories: quality, supply interruption, safety, environmental, and cost of emergency repair
Score each major asset for likelihood of failure from condition, age, history, and duty
Score each asset for consequence of failure, including whether redundancy exists and how long repair would take in winter
Combine likelihood and consequence into a risk rank and list the top risks with their evidence
Have operations and maintenance challenge the ranking in a workshop before it is accepted
Use the accepted ranking to sequence renewals and to set spares and contingency plans for the highest risks

tasks.explanation: Criticality ranking combines likelihood with consequence and winter repair reality, and it is challenged by the people who run the assets before it governs spending.

tasks.prompt: Order a growth and capacity planning study for treatment.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional fast growing utility in Manitoba testing when its plant runs out of capacity under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: demand forecast built through expansion triggers adopted.

cards.label: Build a demand forecast from population, per capita use, industrial commitments, and peaking factors in general terms
Rate the firm capacity of each process step with the largest unit out of service, in the coldest design condition
Find the year each step reaches its firm capacity and identify the true bottleneck step
Develop expansion options for the bottleneck with staging that matches the forecast growth rate
Set decision triggers based on measured demand, so expansion starts on evidence and not on forecast alone
Adopt the triggers and review measured demand against them every year at management review

tasks.explanation: Capacity planning rates firm capacity in the coldest condition and starts expansion on measured demand triggers, so the utility is neither early nor caught short.

tasks.prompt: Order a water master plan update for a regional utility.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional regional utility in British Columbia updating a ten year old master plan under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: old plan reviewed through the updated plan adopted as the planning basis.

cards.label: Review the old plan forecasts against what actually happened to demand, source quality, and growth
Update the technical basis: source capacity, treatment capacity, storage, and quality strategy
Reassess the risks the old plan carried and add new ones, including climate and watershed change
Develop the recommended program of studies, projects, and policy actions with sequencing
Consult the governing body and affected communities on the draft program before finalizing
Adopt the updated master plan and use it as the single basis for capital plans and development approvals

tasks.explanation: A master plan update starts by scoring the old forecasts against reality, because a plan that never checks its own accuracy repeats its errors at larger scale.

tasks.prompt: Order a capital funding and reserve strategy for treatment renewal.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Alberta aligning its reserves with its twenty year renewal needs under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: renewal needs profiled through a reserve policy adopted and reported annually.

cards.label: Profile the renewal spending the capital plan requires year by year over the planning horizon
Inventory current reserves, debt room in general terms, and known external funding programs
Model contribution options that smooth the funding profile instead of spiking in peak project years
Present the options and their long term effects to the governing body in plain language
Adopt a reserve policy with a target range and the conditions for drawing on it
Report reserve position against the policy every year and adjust contributions when the capital plan changes

tasks.explanation: A reserve strategy smooths renewal funding across decades and ties contributions to the capital plan, so one large project year cannot destabilize the utility.

tasks.prompt: Order a value engineering review for a major treatment project.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Saskatchewan reviewing the design of a major plant expansion before tender under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: design functions listed through accepted savings carried into the design.

cards.label: List the functions the design must deliver, separating required performance from preferred features
Bring in reviewers who were not on the design team, including an operator from a comparable plant
Generate alternatives for the highest cost functions and screen them for quality and operability risk
Evaluate the surviving alternatives on lifecycle performance in general terms, not first cost alone
Recommend the alternatives that keep every required function and record why each rejected one was rejected
Carry the accepted alternatives into the design and track the realized effect through construction

tasks.explanation: Value engineering protects required functions first and judges alternatives on lifecycle performance, so savings never come from quietly deleting operability.

tasks.prompt: Order a post project evaluation for a completed treatment upgrade.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Manitoba reviewing a completed filtration upgrade one year after start up under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: project objectives recalled through lessons adopted into the next project.

cards.label: Restate the original objectives, budget in general terms, schedule, and performance guarantees of the project
Measure actual performance against each objective using a full year of operating data
Interview operators and maintainers on what works, what is hard to run, and what they would change
Identify the causes of every significant variance, separating design, construction, and start up causes
Write the lessons as specific changes to the utility design standards and project process
Adopt the standard changes and brief the team starting the next major project on the evaluation

tasks.explanation: Post project evaluation waits for a year of operating data and turns findings into changed standards, so the next project inherits lessons instead of repeating them.
